content: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) is a condition characterized by the failure of the pulmonary circulation to transition from the fetal to the postnatal state. This results in persistently elevated pulmonary arterial pressure and an inability to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance after birth. PPHN is associated with impaired oxygenation and contributes significantly to neonatal mortality and morbidity. Prostanoids and their analogues, such as iloprost, treprostinil, and beraprost, are hypothesized to be potential therapeutic agents for PPHN due to their ability to dilate pulmonary blood vessels and modulate immune responses. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of prostanoids and their analogues in reducing mortality and the need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) in neonates with PPHN. The secondary objective was to assess their efficacy and safety in reducing neonatal complications, such as necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), chronic lung disease (CLD), retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), and periventricular leukomalacia (PVL). Additionally, the study aimed to determine whether these agents could shorten hospital stays, reduce the duration of mechanical ventilation, and improve neurodevelopmental outcomes. The study compared the use of prostanoids and their analogues, at any dosage or duration, against standard treatments without these agents, placebo, or inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) therapy. It also examined the use of prostanoids and their analogues as an adjunct therapy to iNO in cases of refractory PPHN, compared to iNO alone. A comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal standard search strategy. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL were searched up to September 16, 2018. Additional sources included clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles. Authors of previously published studies in this field were also contacted for further information. The inclusion criteria for the study were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that evaluated prostanoids or their analogues in neonates (less than 28 days old) with confirmed or suspected PPHN. The interventions could involve any dose, route of administration, or duration. The standard Cochrane Neonatal methods were used to conduct the systematic review and assess the methodological quality of the included studies. Three independent reviewers screened the titles and abstracts of identified studies, retrieved full-text articles when necessary, and used pre-designed forms for trial inclusion, exclusion, and data extraction. The GRADE approach was planned to assess the quality of evidence. No eligible neonatal trials were identified that evaluated prostanoids or their analogues as sole therapeutic agents for the treatment of PPHN. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence to support the use of prostanoids or their analogues as standalone pulmonary vasodilators for the treatment of PPHN in neonates. They emphasized the need for well-designed, adequately powered, randomized, multi-center trials to establish the safety and efficacy of these agents. Future research should investigate different preparations, doses, and routes of administration of prostanoids and their analogues. Additionally, these trials should evaluate both short-term outcomes and long-term neurodevelopmental and pulmonary outcomes.
